Mini project · 10% · Teams of 3 (one team of 4)

Mini project: an NLP web app, built with a coding agent

In one week, your team builds a working web app for a business problem. It uses a BERT model you fine-tune yourselves and a large language model (LLM) through the Groq API. You write little of the code by hand: a coding agent writes it, and you direct, test and explain it.

The deal

  • Assigned Workshop 9
  • Build one week
  • Presented Workshop 10
  • Teams 5 of 3 and 1 of 4, same scope for all
  • Marks 10, all from the presentation

There are six topics, one per team. Each team ranks its top three, and topics are given out from those choices.

What every project must have

The app

Front end, back end, database

  • A React front end (start from Vite)
  • A FastAPI back end in Python
  • A Postgres database: Neon, added in one click from the Vercel Marketplace
  • Deployed on Vercel, at a public link

The NLP

Two models, two jobs

  • A BERT model you fine-tune on your task, running inside your back end
  • One feature that uses an LLM through the Groq API
  • A test that compares the two on the same task (see Evaluation)

The way you work

A coding agent and its skills

  • A coding agent writes most of the code. Claude Code is recommended; Codex and others are allowed.
  • You follow the five required steps in How you work
  • Every step leaves a file in your repo

No login is needed. One demo user is enough.

The six topics

Four topics classify text: they put each text into one of a fixed set of labels. Two pull details out of text: they label each word as, say, an amount or a date. This is called named-entity recognition (NER).

The starter datasets are suggestions. You may use a different public dataset, or ask the LLM to label data for you (see Data).

1. Bank support desk

A bank's support team gets thousands of messages a day. Your app sorts each new message into the right queue, and drafts a reply the agent can edit and send.

BERT task Classification into 77 query types (card lost, transfer failed, …)
Starter data Banking77 on Hugging Face
LLM feature Drafts a reply from a short FAQ you write for the bank
Database Messages, their predicted type, status (open, replied), replies
Stretch A page showing how many messages of each type arrived each day

2. Review insights for a D2C brand

A direct-to-consumer (D2C) brand sells online and reads every review it gets. Your app tags each review with what it talks about and whether it is positive or negative, then sums up the week.

BERT task Classification into an aspect (delivery, quality, price, packaging, service) and whether it is positive or negative
Starter data A Flipkart product reviews dataset on Kaggle, with the aspects labelled by the LLM
LLM feature A weekly "top 3 issues" report, and a suggested public reply to any review
Database Reviews, their labels, weekly reports
Stretch Upload a CSV of new reviews, and a chart of each aspect over time

3. Resume screener

A recruiter has 200 resumes for one job. Your app pulls out skills, degrees, colleges and past employers, and compares each resume with the job description.

BERT task NER: skills, degree, college, company, years of experience
Starter data A resume NER dataset on Kaggle or Hugging Face
LLM feature A short fit summary against the job description, and five interview questions for the gaps
Database Job descriptions, candidates, the details pulled from each resume
Stretch Upload a PDF resume instead of pasting text

4. UPI and bank SMS spend tracker

Every UPI payment sends you an SMS. Your app reads pasted SMS messages, pulls out the amount, the merchant, the date and the account, and answers questions about your spending.

BERT task NER: amount, merchant, date, account
Starter data SMS messages you generate with the LLM in many bank formats, and then check by hand
LLM feature Answers questions in plain English, such as "How much did I spend on food delivery in October?"
Database Transactions, merchants, categories
Stretch A chart of monthly spend by category

5. Market news mood board

An investor follows ten Nifty stocks. Your app scores each news headline as positive, negative or neutral for the company, and writes a short morning brief for each stock.

BERT task Classification: positive, negative, neutral
Starter data Financial PhraseBank on Hugging Face, plus Indian headlines you label
LLM feature A three-line morning brief for each stock that names the headlines it used
Database Watchlist, headlines, scores, briefs
Stretch Fetch headlines from a news RSS feed every morning with a Vercel cron job

6. Scam message checker

People forward suspicious SMS and WhatsApp messages to family. Your app tells them whether a message is a scam, which kind (KYC update, fake job, lottery, parcel, loan), and what to do.

BERT task Classification: genuine, or one of five scam types
Starter data The SMS Spam Collection (UCI), with scam types labelled by the LLM, plus Indian examples you add
LLM feature Explains the red flags in the message and what the user should do next
Database Checked messages, their labels, how often each scam type appears
Stretch Messages in Hinglish (Hindi written in English letters), using a multilingual BERT

Data

You can get labelled data in two ways:

  • A public dataset that already has labels, like the starter datasets above.
  • Labels from the LLM. Give the Groq LLM your texts and ask it for a label for each one. BERT then learns from those labels. A big, slow model teaches a small, fast one.

Either way, build a test set by hand: 150 to 200 examples whose labels your team has checked one by one. Never train on it.

Never send personal data

Use public or made-up texts only. No real phone numbers, account numbers or names of real customers, in training data or in the demo.

The BERT model

  1. Fine-tune a small BERT, such as DistilBERT, on a free GPU in Google Colab or Kaggle. For NER, fine-tune it for token classification.
  2. Export it to ONNX. ONNX is a file format for models that runs without PyTorch. PyTorch is too large for Vercel's 500 MB limit, and ONNX is not.
  3. Shrink it (quantise it to 8-bit numbers), so the model file is under about 100 MB.
  4. Run it in your back end with onnxruntime. If this fails, you may host the model on a free Hugging Face Space and call it from your back end.

Hand in the training notebook. Put the model file on the Hugging Face Hub, or in your repo if it is small enough.

The LLM

  • Use the Groq API. Your free key has rate limits, so pick a small, fast model for most calls. See the Groq model list.
  • The key lives only in the back end, as a Vercel environment variable. It must never be in the React code or in the repo.
  • Save LLM answers in the database, so the same question is not sent twice.
  • The LLM feature must be useful to the user of your app, not decoration.

Evaluation

On your hand-checked test set, compare:

Model What it is
Your fine-tuned BERT the model in your app
The Groq LLM, zero-shot the LLM with your label list in the prompt and no examples

Report accuracy (the share of labels that are right) and macro F1 for each. F1 combines precision and recall for one label; macro F1 is the average over all labels, so rare labels count as much as common ones. Add the time each model takes for one text.

Then say in one sentence which model you would put in production for this task, and why.

How you work

Install Matt Pocock's skills for your coding agent. In Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills
/plugin install mattpocock-skills@mattpocock

For other agents, run npx skills add mattpocock/skills.

Five steps are required. Each one leaves something in your repo that you show in the presentation.

Step What you do What it leaves in the repo
1. Grill the idea Run the grilling skill: the agent asks you questions about the app until every decision is made docs/grilling.md, the questions and your answers
2. Name things Run the domain-modeling skill to agree the words your app uses (ticket, queue, reply…) CONTEXT.md
3. Plan Turn the decisions into a product requirements document (PRD) and split it into GitHub issues docs/prd.md and the issues
4. Build test-first Run the tdd skill for the back end: write a failing test, make it pass, tidy the code Tests, and commits that show a test before the code
5. Review Run the code-review skill before your final merge, and fix what it finds docs/review.md

prototype (for trying out screens) and diagnosing-bugs are optional.

You must be able to explain the code

The agent may write every line. In the questions, any member may be asked what any part of the app does, and why.

A suggested week

Day Work
1 Grill the idea, write CONTEXT.md, the PRD and the issues. Set up the starter repo.
2 Get the data, build the test set, fine-tune BERT, export it to ONNX.
3 to 5 Build the features issue by issue, tests first. Deploy to Vercel early, on day 3.
6 Finish the LLM feature and the evaluation. Deploy again.
7 Code review, fixes, and a full rehearsal on the live link.

The starter repo

project-starter/ in your course folder has the stack already wired up: React with Vite, FastAPI, the database connection, an ONNX model endpoint, a Groq endpoint, the Vercel settings, and a CLAUDE.md that tells the agent the rules of this project. Copy it into a new GitHub repo for your team, and follow its README.

The presentation

12 minutes of presenting, then 5 minutes of questions. Every member speaks.

  1. The problem and who uses the app
  2. A live demo on your Vercel link, not on your laptop
  3. Your BERT model and the evaluation table
  4. Your repo: the grilling notes, CONTEXT.md, the issues, a test-first commit and the review

Share your GitHub repo with the instructor before the presentation.

Marks

Part Marks
Live demo: the app works end to end on the Vercel link 3
BERT: fine-tuning, ONNX export and the evaluation 2
How you worked: the five steps and what they left in the repo 2
LLM feature: useful, with the key kept safe 1.5
Questions: each member answers at least one, marked for each member 1.5

The first four parts, 8.5 marks, are the same for everyone in the team. The questions, 1.5 marks, are marked for each member.
